title_en: James Robinson on What It Looks Like When a State is Failing
title_zh: 詹姆斯·罗宾逊谈一个国家正在失败时是什么样子
subtitle_zh: 《国家为什么会失败》合著者、2024 年诺贝尔经济学奖得主詹姆斯·罗宾逊（James A. Robinson）做客在芝加哥现场录制的 Odd Lots，与主持人乔·魏森塔尔、崔西·阿洛韦讨论包容性制度与攫取性制度、美国是否正在失败、中国的增长、AI 与创造性破坏。
summary_zh: 本期在 Chicago 现场录制的 Odd Lots 中，Tracy Alloway 与 Joe Weisenthal 请来 University of Chicago 教授、2024 年诺贝尔经济学奖得主、《Why Nations Fail》合著者 James A. Robinson，讨论一个国家「正在失败」时是什么样子。Robinson 的核心框架是：社会经济成功取决于制度（institutions）——把人们的精力引向创新、创业与创造力的规则；美国历史上拥有创造广泛机会的「包容性制度」（inclusive institutions），而委内瑞拉等国则陷入只服务狭隘派系（如 chavistas）的「攫取性制度」（extractive institutions）。他判断美国「还不是」失败国家，Trump 现象更多是民众不满的症状，并强调好的经济政策本质上是政治的下游产物、需要政治支撑；他借助「关键节点」（critical junctures）与北美、拉美殖民史的对比解释制度分野。节目还谈及中国从攫取性向包容性制度转型带来的增长、择优精英制（meritocracy）与「反俘获」特性、Elon Musk 式财富与经典「寡头」的区别，以及 AI 与创造性破坏。Robinson 更分享用 AI 分析数字化政治哲学文本、研究 17 世纪英国 Hobbes 与 Locke 的观念如何影响行动，并提醒关注选举的真实性（veracity）——是一集从制度经济学视角审视当下的深谈。

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
turns.zh: 彭博音频工作室（Bloomberg Audio Studios）。

turns.en: Podcasts. Radio. News.
turns.zh: 播客。电台。新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to a very special episode of the Odd Lots podcast taped live in Chicago. I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听《Odd Lots》播客一期非常特别的节目，本期是在芝加哥现场录制的。我是崔西·阿洛韦（Tracy Alloway）。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是乔·魏森塔尔（Joe Weisenthal）。

turns.en: Joe, there's a lot to talk about when it comes to institutional failures nowadays.
turns.zh: 乔，说到制度失灵（institutional failure），如今可聊的话题实在太多了。

turns.en: Yeah, absolutely true. You know, there's a lot of people, they talk about geopolitics a lot. And of course, there's multiple wars going on. But I also think that if you're in the markets these days, Just thinking about the economy, you actually just have to talk about politics, politics.
turns.zh: 是啊，一点没错。你知道，很多人一直在大谈地缘政治，而且眼下确实有好几场战争在打。但我还认为，如果你如今身在市场之中，仅仅去思考经济本身，你其实就绕不开政治——政治。

turns.en: You really do. And so I'm very happy to say that we have the perfect guest, someone who's actually never been on the show before. But I think a lot of listeners will have heard of him because not only is he a Nobel Prize winner, he is also the author of a very famous book that you and I have probably read a couple of times now called Why Nations Fail. So we're going to be speaking with James Robinson. He is, of course, a professor at the University of Chicago. Hope you enjoy the conversation. Well, Professor Robinson, thank you so much for joining us. Really appreciate it.
turns.zh: 确实绕不开。所以我很高兴地说，我们请到了最完美的嘉宾，一位其实从未上过我们节目的人。但我想很多听众都听说过他，因为他不仅是诺贝尔奖得主，还写了一本非常有名的书，你和我大概都已经读过好几遍了，书名叫《国家为什么会失败》（Why Nations Fail）。所以我们将与詹姆斯·罗宾逊（James Robinson）对话。他当然是芝加哥大学的教授。希望你喜欢这场对话。好的，罗宾逊教授，非常感谢您加入我们，真的很感激。

turns.en: My pleasure.
turns.zh: 我的荣幸。

turns.en: Why do nations fail?
turns.zh: 国家为什么会失败？

turns.en: No.
OK, let me ask the other obvious question right now. I'm just going to get into it. Is the US a failing nation?
turns.zh: 好吧，那我现在就问另一个显而易见的问题。我就直接切入正题了：美国是一个正在失败的国家吗？

turns.en: How long do we have? I know. Okay, good. Not yet. Not yet. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我们有多少时间？我知道。好，行。还没有。还没有。是的。

turns.en: Wait, I have one more random question. Do you call yourself a Nobel Prize winner, or do you say, like, you're a Nobel Prize winner, right? I think it's a real Nobel Prize.
turns.zh: 等等，我还有一个不着调的问题。您会自称是诺贝尔奖得主吗？还是说您会说“你是诺贝尔奖得主，对吧”？我觉得这算是个货真价实的诺贝尔奖。

turns.en: Well, you know, there's some debate about that. I know.
turns.zh: 嗯，这个嘛，关于这一点还有些争议。我知道。

turns.en: Because Alfred Nobel didn't actually specify a prize for.
turns.zh: 因为阿尔弗雷德·诺贝尔（Alfred Nobel）当初其实并没有设立一个针对……

turns.en: Economics, you know, and it came later on. Yeah. So, you know.
turns.zh: ……经济学的奖项，你知道，这个奖是后来才有的。是的。所以，你懂的。

turns.en: It's a Nobel Prize. You're a Nobel Prize winner.
turns.zh: 它就是诺贝尔奖。您就是诺贝尔奖得主。

turns.en: I think you should just go for it.
turns.zh: 我觉得您就大方承认好了。

turns.en: Yeah. I've got the badge. Oh, there you go. All right. The U.S.
turns.zh: 是啊，我有那枚徽章。哦，给你。好吧。美国……

turns.en: Is not a failed state or failed nation.
turns.zh: ……不是一个失败国家，也不是一个已经失败的国家。

turns.en: Is it failing?
turns.zh: 那它正在失败吗？

turns.en: No, I mean, you know, by failure, you know, we're really talking about economic failure, economic success. Failure is a big word. It covers lots of things. So, you know, my work is really about economics and about how society's who succeed economically do so because they create institutions, sets of institutions, kind of rules that channel people's energy in directions which are socially beneficial, innovation, entrepreneurship, creativity. But those energies can be channeled in many different ways. And I think what you see in the United States historically is you've had very important what we call inclusive institutions, you know, institutions, rules that are created, very broad-based patterns of incentives and opportunities, economic success, you know, and poor countries, like Venezuela, say, went into decline because they created the.
turns.zh: 不，我是说，谈到“失败”，我们真正讨论的是经济上的失败、经济上的成功。“失败”是个很大的词，涵盖很多东西。所以，你知道，我的研究其实是关于经济学的，关于一个社会如何在经济上取得成功——它们之所以成功，是因为它们创建了制度（institutions），也就是一整套规则，把人们的精力引导到对社会有益的方向上去：创新、创业、创造力。但这些精力可以被引向许多不同的方向。我认为，从历史上看，美国拥有的是我们所说的非常重要的“包容性制度”（inclusive institutions），也就是那些被创造出来的、形成非常广泛的激励与机会格局的制度与规则，从而带来经济成功。而像委内瑞拉这样的穷国之所以走向衰落，是因为它们创建了……

turns.en: Opposite, which we call extractive institutions.
turns.zh: ……相反的东西，我们称之为“攫取性制度”（extractive institutions）。

turns.en: So institutions that don't create broad-based opportunities or incentives. They create incentives of very narrow standards cliques, the chavistas, you know, and.
turns.zh: 也就是那些不创造广泛机会或激励的制度。它们只为非常狭隘的派系小圈子——比如查韦斯派（the chavistas）——创造激励，而且……

turns.en: Most people are just excluded from opportunities.
turns.zh: ……绝大多数人则干脆被排除在机会之外。

turns.en: So I think the history of the US, you know, has been a remarkable success story, but I think, you know, as we point out in our work, in any society, there's always challenges to inclusive institutions. Some people were doing very well in Venezuela out of that system. So I think, you know, there's always challenges, and there's been a history of challenges in the United States, by the way.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，美国的历史是一部非凡的成功故事。但正如我们在研究中指出的，在任何社会里，包容性制度总会面临挑战。在委内瑞拉，也有一些人从那套体制中获益良多。所以我认为，挑战始终存在；顺便说一句，美国历史上也一直有挑战。

turns.en: You know, it's not a simple... You know, good guy, bad guy story.
turns.zh: 你知道，这并不是一个简单的……不是那种好人对坏人的故事。

turns.en: But the thrust of your work, if I understand it, is that typically in economics, when we talk about what's good economic policy, it's like, well, maybe we should have an independent central bank. Maybe we should have a tax system that doesn't penalize productivity, et cetera.
turns.zh: 但如果我理解得没错，您研究的核心论点是：在经济学里，当我们谈论什么是好的经济政策时，通常会说“嗯，也许我们应该有一家独立的中央银行”“也许我们的税制不应该惩罚生产率”等等。

turns.en: And all that may be true. But all of this is downstream, essentially, from politics, right?
turns.zh: 这些可能都对。但所有这些本质上都是政治的下游产物，对吧？

turns.en: Is this the idea that, like, there is no way to just, like, set up, write down a list of good economic policies if the institutions and politics.
turns.zh: 这是不是意味着，如果制度和政治环境本身并不具备……

turns.en: Aren't there in the first place to be conducive to it?
turns.zh: ……一开始就不具备支持这些政策的条件，那你就根本没办法只是列出一份“好的经济政策清单”？

turns.en: Yes, absolutely. Great.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。很好。

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: I mean, I think all that, you know, that stuff about economic policy and economic institutions are all important.
turns.zh: 我是说，我认为那些关于经济政策和经济制度的东西都很重要。

turns.en: But the politics has to support that. Absolutely. Yeah.
turns.zh: 但政治必须支持这些东西。绝对的。是的。

turns.en: How did you actually develop that approach? Because when we think about economics, I mean, we often think of traditional economics as a model that says if x happens, then y is the result. It's all very formulaic versus your approach that really emphasizes, I guess, the politics, the institutional strength. And you also emphasize, I guess, critical junctures in history where things could have gone either way.
turns.zh: 您究竟是怎么形成这套研究路径的？因为我们想到经济学时，往往会把传统经济学想象成一种模型：如果发生X，结果就是Y，非常公式化。而您的方法真正强调的是——我想是政治、是制度的强度。您还强调历史上的一些“关键节点”（critical junctures），在那些节点上事情本来可能走向任何一个方向。

turns.en: I was trained as an economic theorist.
turns.zh: 我受的是经济理论家的训练。

turns.en: And when I finished my PhD in 1992, I had this kind of epiphany. And I realized I just, I was very interested in these problems, particularly of developing countries. And I realized I just didn't understand anything. And the first place I sort of, so I just needed to start immersing.
turns.zh: 1992年我博士毕业的时候，我有了一种顿悟。我意识到，我对这些问题——尤其是发展中国家的问题——非常感兴趣，但我也意识到自己其实什么都不懂。所以第一个地方，我得开始让自己……

turns.en: Myself in some sense.
turns.zh: ……从某种意义上说，把自己沉浸进去。

turns.en: And the first place I did that actually was in Colombia, interestingly enough.
turns.zh: 而我真正开始这么做的第一个地方，说来有趣，其实是哥伦比亚。

turns.en: And when I got to Colombia, I realized I have no way of understanding what's going on here.
turns.zh: 到了哥伦比亚之后，我意识到自己根本没有办法理解那里正在发生什么。

turns.en: And I just had to kind of back up and start asking myself, why do things happen the way they do? And then the politics just looms incredibly large. I think about Venezuela. How can you understand the economic trajectory of Venezuela or all those mistakes without understanding the politics of Chavez and Chavismo or even before that?
turns.zh: 我只能退回来，开始问自己：事情为什么会以这样的方式发生？这样一来，政治就变得无比重要。想想委内瑞拉吧：如果不理解查韦斯（Chávez）和查韦斯主义（Chavismo）的政治，甚至更早之前的政治，你怎么可能理解委内瑞拉的经济轨迹，或者它犯下的那些错误？

turns.en: So all of.
turns.zh: 所以所有这一切……

turns.en: This makes a lot of sense, and I find it very intuitive. But I also have an issue with, I guess I would say there's maybe a certain non-disprovability issue that I think about, which is that you say, okay, here's a rich country like Britain.
turns.zh: 这很有道理，我也觉得很直观。但我有一个疑问，我想说那可能是一种“不可证伪性”的问题：你说，好，这是一个像英国这样的富国……

turns.en: And the U.S.
turns.zh: ……以及美国……

turns.en: That say they must have good institutions.
turns.zh: ……你就说它们一定拥有好的制度。

turns.en: And then here are some countries that are poor, Venezuela, et cetera, Argentina.
turns.zh: 然后这里有一些穷国，比如委内瑞拉等等，还有阿根廷。

turns.en: And you say, oh, they're bad institutions.
turns.zh: 你就说，哦，它们的制度很糟。

turns.en: But if we're only looking at the outcome, how do you actually establish sort of, I guess, a priori that that.
turns.zh: 但如果我们只是在看结果，你又怎么能真正确立——我想是“先验地”（a priori）确立——那……

turns.en: Is the actual thing?
turns.zh: ……就是真正的成因呢？

turns.en: Let's say you didn't know anything about the economy. You were looking at something about a country, but you were not.
turns.zh: 假设你对这个国家的经济一无所知。你在观察一个国家的某些方面，但你并没有……

turns.en: Given privy to GDP growth, anything like that.
turns.zh: ……被告知它的GDP增速之类的信息。

turns.en: Are there other ways to know whether that country has good or bad institutions?
turns.zh: 还有没有别的办法能判断这个国家的制度是好还是坏？

turns.en: I mean, you know, what we got the Nobel Prize for, me and my collaborators, was sort of establishing empirically this connection between institutions and economic development. But, you know, that's a hard question to ask. You know, you could look at life expectancy. You can look at infant mortality. You know, I think when you look at most failing countries failing economically, Yeah, they do badly in terms of income per capita, but they do badly in terms of most socioeconomic outcomes also.
turns.zh: 我是说，你知道，我和我的合作者们获得诺贝尔奖的原因，就是在实证上确立了制度与经济发展之间的这种联系。但这是个很难回答的问题。你可以看预期寿命，可以看婴儿死亡率。我认为，当你观察大多数经济上失败的国家时，是的，它们的人均收入表现很差，但它们在大多数社会经济结果上也都表现很差。

turns.en: You can even look at night light.
turns.zh: 你甚至还可以看夜间灯光。

turns.en: The most famous photograph we have in our book is the Korean peninsula at night.
turns.zh: 我们书里最有名的一张照片，就是夜间的朝鲜半岛。

turns.en: It's getting brighter, the North Korean peninsula.
turns.zh: 那边正在变亮呢，朝鲜半岛。

turns.en: It's getting a little brighter. Maybe the presidential palace in Pyongyang. There's a wave pool.
turns.zh: 确实变亮了一点点。也许只是平壤的总统府。那儿有个造浪泳池。

turns.en: You've mentioned Venezuela a couple of times.
turns.zh: 您提到委内瑞拉好几次了。

turns.en: Can you just.
turns.zh: 能不能请您……

turns.en: Apply your framework for us to Venezuela under, I guess, Chavez and Maduro and then Rodriguez now.
turns.zh: ……用您的框架给我们分析一下委内瑞拉：先是查韦斯（Chávez）、然后是马杜罗（Maduro），再到现在罗德里格斯（Rodríguez）治下的委内瑞拉。

turns.en: Well, I think, you know, that comes into path dependence, as you mentioned. Like, I think, you know, if you look at the history of the Americas, if you look at this economic divergence between North America and Latin America, you know, that's very deeply rooted in history. It's rooted in the way very different types of societies got created in the colonial period. You know, in Latin America, you see societies based on coercion of indigenous people, on slavery, you know, and that created hierarchy, you know, it created very extractive institutions, and that led to poverty, and, you know, I think, you know, if you look at the United States, of course, that's a complicated picture.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为这就涉及你提到的路径依赖（path dependence）。如果你看看美洲的历史，看看北美与拉丁美洲之间的这种经济分流，你会发现它深深植根于历史之中，植根于殖民时期所形成的、非常不同类型的社会。在拉丁美洲，你看到的是建立在胁迫原住民和奴隶制基础上的社会，这就造成了等级制，造成了非常攫取性的制度，进而导致贫困。而如果你看美国，当然，那是一幅复杂的图景。

turns.en: The U.S.
turns.zh: 美国……

turns.en: South had what we would call extractive institutions, but for us, you know, and, of course, the South until very recently was poorer than the rest of the country.
turns.zh: ……南部拥有我们所说的攫取性制度，当然，直到不久前，南方一直比全国其他地区更穷。

turns.en: It was less urbanized.
turns.zh: 它的城市化程度更低。

turns.en: There was less industry, but, you know, the key thing is that When the U.S. institutional framework got kind of definitively set up with the Constitution, it's the North that somehow really created that.
turns.zh: 工业也更少。但关键在于，当美国的制度框架通过宪法被确定性地建立起来时，真正促成这一点的是北方。

turns.en: So there were compromises. Actually, can you explain.
turns.zh: 所以这其中有很多妥协。其实，能不能请您解释一下……

turns.en: This is a little bit of history, because when they landed in the U.S., they were hoping to replicate the extraction of South America.
turns.zh: ……这段历史：因为他们当初登陆美洲时，是希望复制在南美洲那种掠夺式的做法。

turns.en: It didn't work the same way.
turns.zh: 但结果并不一样。

turns.en: Why?
turns.zh: 为什么？

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, that's a fascinating story that with the Jamestown Colony, the origins of the Jamestown Colony, You know, the colonists came with a model of how you colonize the New World, which is actually completely based.
turns.zh: 是啊，这真是个引人入胜的故事——詹姆斯敦殖民地（Jamestown Colony）、它的起源。你知道，殖民者们带着一套“如何殖民新大陆”的模板过来，而这套模板其实完全是建立在……

turns.en: On the Spanish conquest of Latin America.
turns.zh: ……西班牙对拉丁美洲的征服之上。

turns.en: It's just that you couldn't, there were no indigenous people to exploit in Virginia.
turns.zh: 只是他们做不到——在弗吉尼亚根本没有可供剥削的原住民。

turns.en: And, you know, there's a whole sort of farcical early history where.
turns.zh: 而且，你知道，早期还有一段堪称闹剧的历史……

turns.en: The English settlers tried to, you know, exploiting indigenous people. In the meantime, they didn't bother planting any crops, and two-thirds of them starved to death because their model was, we.
turns.zh: 英国定居者试图去剥削原住民。与此同时，他们压根懒得种任何庄稼，结果三分之二的人被饿死了，因为他们的模式是：我们……

turns.en: Don't work, we exploit the indigenous people.
turns.zh: ……不干活，我们去剥削原住民。

turns.en: And when that model crashed and burned, then they had to kind of experiment with other types of models, including, let's get, we need to get British people to come here. So how do you get them to come? Then they created a much more inclusive set of political and economic institutions because they realized you know of course this was before the slave economy takes off they realized that you know to have a viable economy here we need to get people to come and so then there's this institutional transition you know and virginia creates this legislative assembly with universal male suffrage which is a sort of unprecedented innovation.
turns.zh: 而当这套模式彻底破产之后，他们就不得不去尝试其他类型的模式，包括“我们得让英国人愿意来这里”。那怎么让他们来呢？于是他们创建了一套更具包容性的政治和经济制度，因为他们意识到——你知道，这都发生在奴隶制经济起飞之前——他们意识到，要在这里建立一个可行的经济体，就必须把人吸引过来。于是就出现了这场制度转型：弗吉尼亚建立了一个实行全体男性普选权的立法议会，这是一种前所未有的制度创新。

turns.en: Just going back to Venezuela. So with Rodriguez now, is that system still an extractive system?
turns.zh: 回到委内瑞拉。那么现在罗德里格斯治下，那个体制还是一个攫取性体制吗？

turns.en: Absolutely, yes.
turns.zh: 绝对是，是的。

turns.en: Say more.
turns.zh: 多说一点。

turns.en: We're not doing anything about it, and we should be.
turns.zh: 我们对此什么都没做，而我们本该做点什么。

turns.en: Well, this relationship that now U.S. and Venezuela have.
turns.zh: 那么，如今美国和委内瑞拉之间这种关系……

turns.en: or Marco Rubio and Rodriguez have. Is there an interesting parallel in history? Is this an unusual relationship?
turns.zh: ……或者说马尔科·卢比奥（Marco Rubio）和罗德里格斯之间的关系，在历史上有意思的对照吗？这是一种不同寻常的关系吗？

turns.en: I think it's not so unusual. I mean, I think if you look at the history of U.S. relations with Latin America, you see similar things.
turns.zh: 我认为并不算太不寻常。我是说，如果你回顾美国与拉丁美洲关系的历史，你会看到类似的事情。

turns.en: U.S.
turns.zh: 美国……

turns.en: In the past occupied Haiti and Hispaniola.
turns.zh: ……过去曾占领过海地（Haiti）和伊斯帕尼奥拉岛（Hispaniola）。

turns.en: So There's the United Fruit Company. It's not ridiculously anomalous, no.
turns.zh: 还有联合果品公司（United Fruit Company）。所以这算不上离谱的异类，不是。

turns.en: This is going to be a devil's advocate question.
turns.zh: 下面这会是一个唱反调的问题（devil's advocate）。

turns.en: I just want to make that very clear before I say it. But is there a path where accountability to the U.S. for Venezuela could lead to more domestic, democratic accountability?
turns.zh: 在我问之前我想把这一点讲清楚。但是，委内瑞拉对美国负责，有没有一条路径最终能走向更多的国内民主问责？

turns.en: In Venezuela? Yeah. I think it's very difficult. for any outside power to sort out these problems, you know, in some sense.
turns.zh: 在委内瑞拉？嗯，我认为，从某种意义上说，任何外部大国都很难去解决这些问题。

turns.en: Like, what my research shows is that, you know, countries that make a transition from more extractive to more inclusive institutions, they do it because they find a way themselves or they sort it out themselves, you know, like Chile, for example. So, you know, Chile is by far the most successful economy in Latin America. It has the best functioning institutions. That was the Chileans that did that, you know. So I don't think the U.S. can really solve that problem in Venezuela? You know, I think they could probably not exacerbate it, but I'm not sure that they're able to solve that problem. And I think it's an interesting question. You know, so I wouldn't say, you know, I wouldn't say Latin America is the way it is because of the way the United States. Sometimes it's interacted in a very dysfunctional way, but I don't think the United States is responsible for the problem.
turns.zh: 比如，我的研究表明，那些从较为攫取性的制度转向较为包容性制度的国家，它们之所以成功，是因为它们自己找到了办法、自己把问题理顺了，比如智利（Chile）。智利是拉丁美洲迄今为止最成功的经济体，它拥有运转得最好的制度，而那是智利人自己做到的。所以我不认为美国真能解决委内瑞拉的问题。我认为他们大概能做到不去加剧它，但我不确定他们有能力解决那个问题。我觉得这是个有意思的问题。所以我不会说拉丁美洲之所以是今天这个样子，是因为美国——尽管美国有时以一种非常失灵的方式介入过——但我不认为美国要为这个问题负责。

turns.en: That's much more deeply rooted historically.
turns.zh: 这个问题的历史根源要深得多。

turns.en: You know, you have a very big fan of these days, the new president of Syria, I believe, who used to be a jihadi not that long ago.
turns.zh: 你知道，如今您有一位非常忠实的粉丝，我想是叙利亚的新总统，他不久前还是一名圣战分子（jihadi）。

turns.en: Is now like Mr.
turns.zh: 现在却成了……

turns.en: Like neoliberal, like going and like speaking at like, I don't know, like the Atlantic Institute in Brookings. And he's like, I read why nations fail and stuff like that.
turns.zh: ……新自由主义先生，跑去在——我不知道——大西洋研究所（Atlantic Institute）或者布鲁金斯学会（Brookings）之类的地方发表演讲，然后说“我读过《国家为什么会失败》”这种话。

turns.en: First of all, that's, what's that like?
turns.zh: 首先，那是什么感觉？

turns.en: I'm waiting for the call. He hasn't called me yet.
turns.zh: 我在等他的电话呢。他还没打给我。

turns.en: Let's say he does call.
turns.zh: 假设他真的打电话来了。

turns.en: He's like, I really like your book, but now I've got to put some of this institution building into practice. Is there a model for like, okay, let's build some durable, inclusive institutions that he could reach for? Is there another country where it's like, you know what, follow their playbook.
turns.zh: 他说“我真的很喜欢你的书，但现在我得把其中一些制度建设的想法付诸实践”。有没有一个现成的模板可以让他拿来用，比如“好，我们来建立一些持久的、包容性的制度”？有没有哪个国家可以让他说“你知道吗，就照着他们的剧本做”……

turns.en: That worked.
turns.zh: ……而且那套剧本确实奏效了？

turns.en: I think that's very complicated because I think what our research shows and the way we've approached this is You know, if you want to compare all these different countries and today and historically, you need a sort of– you need concepts which are sort of flexible enough to cover a lot of details. You know, if I talk about inclusive and extractive institutions, of course, the details of those things are very different. But if you're in the business of actually advising Syria, which I'm not in this business of advising– Go to Siri or.
turns.zh: 我觉得那非常复杂，因为我们的研究以及我们处理这个问题的方式是：如果你想比较今天以及历史上的所有这些不同国家，你需要一些足够灵活、能够涵盖大量细节的概念。如果我谈包容性制度和攫取性制度，当然，这些东西的具体细节是非常不同的。但如果你的工作是真正去给叙利亚提建议——我并不干这一行——那你去问 Siri 或者……

turns.en: Anywhere else, actually. You know, then all the details become.
turns.zh: ……其实去问别的谁都行。你知道，那样一来所有的细节就变得至关重要。

turns.en: If he's listening, your phone line is open.
turns.zh: 如果他在听的话，您的电话随时为他开着。

turns.en: I'm like, you know, what I'm happy to do is, you know, people want to talk to me and they want to ask me questions about what I know and what models might be helpful for them.
turns.zh: 我是这样想的：我愿意做的是——如果有人想跟我聊聊，想问问我一些我知道的东西，问哪些模型可能对他们有帮助……

turns.en: I'm happy to engage at that level.
turns.zh: ……我很乐意在这个层面上交流。

turns.en: But, you know, to do anything useful for Siri, you'd have to understand the details of the politics and the institutions and the society.
turns.zh: 但是，你知道，要想为叙利亚真正做点有用的事，你就必须理解其政治、制度和社会的具体细节。

turns.en: And, of course, I don't. Well, this kind of.
turns.zh: 而我当然并不了解。嗯，这就有点……

turns.en: Gets to one of the criticisms from your famous non-fans, which was Bill Gates. So Bill Gates wrote a book review of why nations fail, and he kind of criticized you for explaining why strong institutions matter, but not explaining how to actually get them. What's your response to that particular criticism?
turns.zh: 这就引出了您那位著名的“非粉丝”对您的批评之一，那就是比尔·盖茨（Bill Gates）。比尔·盖茨为《国家为什么会失败》写过一篇书评，他大致上批评您解释了强制度为什么重要，却没有解释如何真正建立起这种制度。对这一具体的批评，您怎么回应？

turns.en: Well, you know, institutions are, you know, like they're an outcome of a sort of political equilibrium, I would say. So our research has been about trying to describe those equilibria and trying to describe historically why some parts of the world got into the situation that they did. And so changing them, that's something completely different. So we try to describe historically why societies changed and how they changed. But the idea that there'd just be some lever that you pull in Syria, that seems a bit kind of simplistic to me, you know, so I, you know, I, you know, he has a very simple view of the world, I suppose, you know, he sort of thinks, he thinks like an engineer, you know, but social systems are not like, you know, they're not like computer programs.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为制度可以说是一种政治均衡（political equilibrium）的结果。所以我们的研究一直是试图描述这些均衡，并从历史上说明世界上某些地区为什么会陷入它们所处的那种境地。因此，改变制度是完全不同的另一回事。我们尝试从历史上描述社会为什么会改变、又是如何改变的。但那种认为在叙利亚只要拉动某个杠杆就能解决问题的想法，在我看来有点过于简单化了。所以，我想他对世界有一种非常简单的看法，他是像工程师那样思考的，但社会系统并不像……它们不像计算机程序。

turns.en: So we started off with like the very aggressive loaded question, is US failing, you know.
turns.zh: 我们一开始就抛出了那个非常咄咄逼人、带诱导性的问题：美国是不是正在失败。

turns.en: And now we return to it.
turns.zh: 现在我们回到这个问题上。

turns.en: Well, no, yes, kind of. We look at the United States these days, and.
turns.zh: 呃，不，是的，算是吧。看看今天的美国……

turns.en: People are certainly, like, you know, setting aside failing. There are institutions, like, people are worried about the future of an independent central bank. People are worried about, like, is our voting system going to be durable and so forth. Like, are there patterns of this? Does this look like anything familiar when you look across the country of, you know, across the landscape of failed nations?
turns.zh: ……人们当然在担忧——先把“失败”这个词放在一边——就制度而言，人们担心独立的中央银行的未来，人们担心我们的选举制度还能不能持久等等。这些有没有什么模式可循？当你放眼那些失败国家的图景时，美国眼下这个样子看起来像不像什么熟悉的东西？

turns.en: I mean, I think there's lots of problems in this country, honestly. For me, President Trump and all of that, he's a symptom of people's discontent.
turns.zh: 我是说，老实讲，我认为这个国家有很多问题。对我而言，特朗普总统以及那一切，他是民众不满的一种症状。

turns.en: If you look at data on people's.
turns.zh: 如果你看看有关民众……的数据……

turns.en: Trust in institutions in this country, it's absolutely horrifying. So there are real problems here. A lot of people are very unhappy with what's been going on, with their opportunities, with the societies. And in some sense, you could think of this as a big failure of inclusion in this country.
turns.zh: ……看看民众对这个国家制度的信任度数据，那简直令人恐怖。所以这里确实存在真实的问题。很多人对正在发生的一切、对他们拥有的机会、对这个社会都非常不满。从某种意义上说，你可以把这看作是这个国家在“包容”上的一次重大失败。

turns.en: I mean, if you don't have a college degree.
turns.zh: 我是说，如果你没有大学文凭……

turns.en: which is the sort of narrow majority of people in this country, your income is no higher than it was 50 years ago. It's absolutely astonishing. So that's a failure of inclusion. So there are problems with institutions, and they need to be addressed. And I think he's a symptom of there's problems, and we need to solve these problems, and we need to figure out how to solve them.
turns.zh: ……而这个国家里没上大学的人是勉强占多数的那部分人，你的收入并不比50年前更高。这实在令人震惊。所以这就是一种包容的失败。因此制度确实存在问题，必须去解决。我认为他（特朗普）是问题存在的一种症状，我们需要解决这些问题，而且我们需要弄清楚该怎么解决。

turns.en: I'm not sure that he actually has a solution.
turns.zh: 我不确定他真的有一套解决方案。

turns.en: But, you know, in some sense, you have to recognize there's a problem to come up with a solution. And, you know, I don't think President Biden really sort of understood that, you know, and now we see it. And, of course, it's a bit nerve-wracking, you know, because part of this, you know, is a challenge to institutions, for sure.
turns.zh: 但是，从某种意义上说，你得先承认存在问题，才谈得上提出解决方案。我认为拜登总统其实并没有真正理解这一点，而现在我们看到了后果。当然，这有点让人神经紧绷，因为其中一部分确实是对制度的挑战。

turns.en: But then you could say, well.
turns.zh: 但话又说回来，你也可以说，嗯……

turns.en: Institutions aren't working, so let's figure out how to make them better.
turns.zh: ……制度运转不灵了，那我们就想办法把它们变得更好。

turns.en: You mentioned inclusion just then, and part of your framework is this idea of if political power is broadly distributed or not. What if you get a system where everyone gets a vote, but their political choices are ultimately determined by campaign finance and lobbying and who controls the media and the narrative that's being spinned? How does your framework apply to, I guess, what people would call democratic capture nowadays?
turns.zh: 您刚才提到了“包容”，而您框架的一部分就是政治权力是否被广泛分配这个观念。如果出现这样一种体制：每个人都有投票权，但他们的政治选择最终由竞选资金、由游说、由谁控制媒体以及被炮制出来的叙事所决定，那会怎样？您的框架如何适用于如今人们所说的“民主俘获”（democratic capture）？

turns.en: I mean, you know, I think, you know, so I've done a lot of research on this question of, you know, the impact of democracy on kind of public policy.
turns.zh: 我是说，你知道，我在这个问题上做过大量研究，也就是民主对公共政策……

turns.en: And economic growth.
turns.zh: ……和经济增长的影响。

turns.en: And, you know, what we find, I think the evidence is overwhelming that democracy is associated with better public policy, more inclusive public policy, more spending on education, and higher rates of economic.
turns.zh: 我们发现——我认为证据是压倒性的——民主与更好的公共政策、更具包容性的公共政策、更多的教育支出以及更高的经济……

turns.en: Growth, you know.
turns.zh: ……增长率相关联。

turns.en: But that's not to say, you know, that there's democracy varies enormously, you know. There's lots of different sorts of democracies and Some demographies have worked very imperfectly. They could be corrupt. They could be clientelistic. They could be captured. I, you know, and I, so I think like, you know, I do tend to think that there are, those are issues, you know, like the enormous amount of money, you know, hundreds of millions of dollars that's thrown into these elections, you know, is a problem. You know, for me, like the biggest problem with inequality is actually the way it spills over into the political system rather than, you know, just in terms of the economy.
turns.zh: 但这并不是说民主都一样，民主之间的差异极其巨大。有很多种不同的民主，有些民主运转得非常不完善：它们可能是腐败的，可能是庇护主义的（clientelistic），可能被俘获。所以我确实认为这些都是问题，比如砸进这些选举里的巨额资金——数亿美元——就是一个问题。对我而言，不平等最大的问题其实在于它向政治体系的溢出，而不仅仅是在经济层面。

turns.en: Do you think oligarch is a good word to describe– no, a lot of people refer– they talk about Elon Musk and oligarchs.
turns.zh: 您觉得“寡头”（oligarch）是个合适的词吗——不，是很多人——他们会谈到埃隆·马斯克（Elon Musk）和寡头。

turns.en: It's become like a thing in the discourse.
turns.zh: 这在公共讨论里已经成了一种流行说法。

turns.en: Is that a useful term for when we look at the influence of money or extremely wealthy individuals who maybe are politically active, et cetera? Do you find the sort of oligarch framework to be illuminating?
turns.zh: 当我们观察金钱的影响力，或者那些可能在政治上非常活跃的超级富豪时，“寡头”是一个有用的术语吗？您觉得这种寡头框架有启发性吗？

turns.en: I'm not sure it is because– The funny thing about Elon Musk is at the end of the day, he's made all of that money through innovation. And I think people admire that. You've got to admire the guy. He's just so ambitious and driven, and he's producing stuff that people want.
turns.zh: 我不确定它是。因为——关于埃隆·马斯克，有趣的一点是，归根结底，他所有的钱都是通过创新赚来的。我认为人们钦佩这一点。你不得不佩服这个人，他就是那么有野心、有干劲，而且他在生产人们想要的东西。

turns.en: And that's distinct from what we would classically call when we use the word oligarch.
turns.zh: 而这与我们在使用“寡头”这个词时经典所指的东西是不同的。

turns.en: Yeah, I think when people start talking about oligarchs in Russia or oligarchs in Latin America or whatever it is, they think about people who've made their fortune by, you know, currying favor with the government or through monopolies and things like that. So it has this pejorative connotation that I'm not sure, I don't think it's good for society that Elon Musk can freely pour hundreds of millions of dollars into elections, but I think you have to recognize the way the wealth was made.
turns.zh: 是啊，我想当人们开始谈论俄罗斯的寡头或者拉丁美洲的寡头之类时，他们想到的是那些靠巴结政府、靠垄断之类的手段发财的人。所以这个词带有贬义。我不认为马斯克能够自由地向选举中投入数亿美元是件对社会有益的事，但你必须承认这些财富是怎么创造出来的。

turns.en: Actually, now that we're.
turns.zh: 其实，既然我们现在……

turns.en: Talking about Elon Musk creating stuff and subsequent wealth, can you talk about, I guess, industrial capacity? So this is This is a big topic in the U.S. The U.S. wants to build up certain industries, certain strategic industries. We seem to be in competition with China for doing things like semiconductor fabs and that sort of thing. In your framework, how do you sort of clarify, I guess, a government that wants to build capacity in a good faith economic, maybe, you know, democratic way so that the gains flow.
turns.zh: ……正在谈论埃隆·马斯克创造东西以及由此而来的财富，那您能不能谈谈工业产能（industrial capacity）？这在美国是个大话题。美国想要建立起某些产业、某些战略性产业。在半导体晶圆厂之类的事情上，我们似乎在和中国竞争。在您的框架里，您如何厘清这样一个政府：它想以善意的、经济上乃至（你知道）民主的方式来建设产能，好让收益流向……

turns.en: To everyone versus.
turns.zh: ……流向所有人，还是流向……

turns.en: an.
Autocratic or oligarchic state where the wealth accrues to a select few?
turns.zh: ……专制或寡头化的国家，那里的财富归于少数特权阶层？

turns.en: Well, you know, I think there's good arguments for having, you know, various sorts of industrial policies, for instance. And, you know, you see, I mean, there's a lot of economists who say, oh, you know, we can't, you know, the United States can't do that. We can't build up all this industry. But actually, you know, the fact of the matter is, you know, if you look at a place like South Korea, South Korea created from scratch amazingly competitive industry, like shipbuilding industry. Hyundai hadn't built a rowing boat in the late 1960s. And then it started, you know, so it went from nothing to create. So why couldn't the United States do that?
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为有充分的理由支持各种产业政策。你知道，有很多经济学家会说“哦，美国做不到，我们没法把这些产业都建起来”。但事实是，如果你看看韩国（South Korea）这样的地方，韩国从无到有创造出了极具竞争力的产业，比如造船业。现代（Hyundai）在1960年代末连一艘划艇都没造过，然后它就开始做了——从零开始创造出来。那么美国为什么不能这么做呢？

turns.en: Of course it could, actually. But in order to do it, you need to be immensely serious. You need to plan. You need to have strategy. I don't see that.
turns.zh: 当然，其实它完全能做到。但要做到这一点，你必须极其认真：你必须做规划，必须有战略。我看不到这些。

turns.en: How do you ensure that you don't do that in a corrupt way? So for instance, right now, the US government is taking a lot of stakes in different companies. I think it just announced yesterday it was taking a 4% in global foundries.
turns.zh: 你怎么才能确保不是以腐败的方式去做这件事？比如说，眼下美国政府正在入股很多不同的公司。我想就在昨天，它刚刚宣布要入股格芯（GlobalFoundries）4%的股份。

turns.en: And that might be fine.
turns.zh: 这也许没问题。

turns.en: But some people might also worry that maybe the process is corrupt in some way. Maybe we should better understand which companies go up for a government contract bid and that sort of thing. How do you make sure it's fair?
turns.zh: 但也有人可能会担心，这个过程在某种意义上也许是腐败的。也许我们应该更好地了解哪些公司会去竞标政府合同之类的事情。你怎么才能确保它是公平的？

turns.en: Institutions.
turns.zh: 制度。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: Say more.
turns.zh: 多说一点。

turns.en: Just say that it's institutions.
turns.zh: 就只说一句“是制度”？

turns.en: But which institutions?
turns.zh: 但究竟是哪些制度？

turns.en: Which institutions should we most be worrying about, actually?
turns.zh: 其实，我们最应该担心的是哪些制度？

turns.en: That's a question I wanted to ask you.
turns.zh: 这正是我想问你们的问题。

turns.en: Yeah, I think accountability about, you know, that's really about the process through which this is done, how contracts are allocated.
turns.zh: 是啊，我想关键在于问责（accountability），这实际上是关于事情通过什么样的程序来完成、合同如何被分配。

turns.en: You know, that process, you know, I.
turns.zh: 你知道，那个程序……我……

turns.en: Think in the Korean example, When that started, that was done under this sort of military government.
turns.zh: 我认为，在韩国的例子里，当这一切开始时，那是在某种军政府之下完成的。

turns.en: But it was a very different context.
turns.zh: 但那是一个非常不同的环境。

turns.en: It was a geopolitical context where there was this contest with North Korea. It was very pressing for the Korean military to do these things. But it was only sustained because that transition occurred in Korea in the 1980s towards much more democratic accountable governance.
turns.zh: 那是一个地缘政治环境，当时存在与朝鲜的对抗，对韩国军方来说做这些事情非常迫切。但只有因为韩国在1980年代发生了向更加民主、更加可问责的治理的转型，这种增长才得以持续。

turns.en: Then you see economic growth is even faster.
turns.zh: 然后你会看到经济增长甚至更快了。

turns.en: I think one thing we point out in Why Nations Fail is all sorts of things can happen in a transitory way. The Soviet Union even did well transitarily, but you have to sustain it, then the institutions become really important.
turns.zh: 我认为我们在《国家为什么会失败》中指出的一点是：各种事情都可能以短暂的方式发生。就连苏联也曾短暂地表现良好，但你必须让它可持续，这时候制度就变得真正重要了。

turns.en: Well, let's talk about China, because obviously the economy has grown extraordinarily. You said, generally speaking, democracy is good, but it's not.
turns.zh: 那么，我们来谈谈中国，因为显然它的经济增长得非常出色。您说过，一般而言民主是好的，但它并不……

turns.en: Always great and there are ways it could go wrong.
turns.zh: ……总是完美的，而且它有出问题的那些方式。

turns.en: How would you describe the institutional preconditions such that China has seen such extraordinary growth over the last few decades?
turns.zh: 您会如何描述中国在过去几十年里实现如此非凡增长所依赖的制度前提条件？

turns.en: Well, I think if I look at the economics, then China has flourished because it made this transition from extractive to inclusive institutions you know it's not the genius of the communist party that did that.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果我看经济层面的话，中国之所以繁荣，是因为它完成了从攫取性制度向包容性制度的转型。你知道，这并不是共产党的天才所为。

turns.en: But what are the inclusive people would say what did china has inclusive institutions so like what are the inclusive institutions i.
turns.zh: 但包容性制度究竟是什么？人们会说中国确实有包容性制度，那么这些包容性制度到底是什么？我……

turns.en: Think there's two things to separate here one is the economics and one is the politics okay so the politics is sort of unreformed you know we would say that's extractive institutions so the paradox is you know how you have that with inclusive institutions i think you know the whole history of the chinese transition from 1978 is the Is the Communist Party kind of detaching itself from the economy to allow entrepreneurship, to allow business to start? So how is that combination possible? And what our theory says is that there's many instances of that historically. Even the Soviet Union, for example, grew very rapidly for 50 years. So we would say that's a sort of anomalous, it's a kind of, we call that extractive growth. And it'll go off the rails. I don't know how.
turns.zh: 我认为这里有两件事需要分开来看：一是经济，一是政治。好，政治层面基本上没有改革，我们会说那是攫取性制度。所以悖论就在于：这样的政治怎么和包容性制度并存？我认为，从1978年开始的中国转型的整段历史，就是共产党在经济上某种程度地“脱身”，允许创业、允许办企业。那么这种组合为什么可能？我们的理论认为，历史上有很多这样的例子。比如苏联也曾高速增长了50年。所以我们会说那是一种反常现象，我们称之为“攫取性增长”（extractive growth）。它会脱轨的。我不知道它会怎么……

turns.en: It will go off the rails.
turns.zh: ……它会脱轨。

turns.en: You're making a call here.
turns.zh: 您这可是下了个判断。

turns.en: Absolutely, yeah.
turns.zh: 绝对的，是的。

turns.en: And I think the basic reason for that is obvious, which is power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. And you don't have to go very far back in Chinese history to see that.
turns.zh: 我认为根本原因很明显：权力倾向于导致腐败，而绝对的权力导致绝对的腐败。你不必在中国历史上回溯很久就能看到这一点。

turns.en: The argument you make in the book is that if you have maybe more economic inclusion without political inclusiveness, then you get this elite that basically stimmies creative destruction of industries. So you don't get as much evolution in the economy as you would otherwise. And for that reason in the book, you say that you think eventually China's growth is going to slow down. I mean, we're here in 2026. It's below 5% in the first half of 2026, but like, you know, 4.6% or whatever is still pretty good.
turns.zh: 您在书里提出的论点是，如果有了更多的经济包容，却没有政治上的包容，你就会得到这样一个精英阶层，他们基本上会扼杀产业的“创造性破坏”（creative destruction）。因此经济中的演进就不会像本来可能的那样多。也正因如此，您在书中说，您认为中国的增长最终会放缓。我是说，我们现在身处2026年，2026年上半年的增速低于5%，但4.6%左右其实还是挺不错的。

turns.en: What would make you think that.
turns.zh: 什么会让您觉得……

turns.en: You were wrong in that creative destruction argument?
turns.zh: ……您在那个创造性破坏的论断上错了？

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, that's a good question.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说，这是个好问题。

turns.en: I mean, you know, I tend to think I'm wrong all the time. You know, I don't admit it in public.
turns.zh: 我是说，我总觉得自己一直是错的，只是我不在公开场合承认罢了。

turns.en: No one's listening to this. This is not being recorded.
turns.zh: 没人在听这段。这没在录音。

turns.en: I mean, I think, you know, like.
turns.zh: 我是说，我认为，你知道，比如……

turns.en: obviously, you know, China is culturally very different, you know, from Western societies. So I think, you know, an interesting line of thought is to say, you know, maybe there's just something culturally different about China, you know, about.
turns.zh: 显然，中国在文化上与西方社会非常不同。所以我认为，一条有意思的思路是说：也许中国就是有一些文化上不同的东西，关于……

turns.en: The history of the state.
turns.zh: ……关于国家的历史。

turns.en: You know, there's no history of accountability, you know, in China, you go back two and a half thousand years, you know, you don't have anything like that. You know, there's a very different notion of state and society in China. So I think, you know, you could imagine that there's, There's something anomalous culturally about this that keeps it going. But I still think.
turns.zh: 你知道，在中国没有问责的历史。你往回看两千五百年，你找不到任何类似的东西。中国对国家与社会有着非常不同的观念。所以我认为，你可以设想这里面存在某种文化上的反常因素，使它得以延续下去。但我仍然认为……

turns.en: Absolute power corrupts absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对的权力导致绝对的腐败。

turns.en: It's going to go off the rails.
turns.zh: 它会脱轨的。

turns.en: It's just a matter of time.
turns.zh: 这只是时间问题。

turns.en: It's interesting, though, because, for example, a few years ago, they had the big crackdown on big tech companies. And Jack Ma was put in his place, etc., This, from the outside, and I'm very unreliable here because I consume a lot of Chinese propaganda on Instagram and stuff.
turns.zh: 不过这也很有意思，因为比如几年前，他们对大型科技公司进行了大整顿，马云（Jack Ma）被“摆正了位置”等等。这是从外部看的，而且我在这一点上非常不可靠，因为我在Instagram之类的平台上消费了大量中国的宣传内容。

turns.en: So I just think everything's going amazing there. Just China, Maxine.
turns.zh: 所以我就觉得那边一切都好得不得了，就是那种“中国样样都好”的感觉。

turns.en: This looks like a political system that's anti-capture, that's maybe avoiding capture more than a democratic institution.
turns.zh: 这看起来像是一个“反俘获”的政治体制，它避免被俘获的能力也许比民主制度还强。

turns.en: That you can get very rich.
turns.zh: 在中国你可以变得非常富有……

turns.en: In China, but it's not easy for the successful businessmen To have much political influence.
turns.zh: ……但成功的商人要拥有多大的政治影响力却并不容易。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.en: And, you know, China does have these advantages. You know, like, I mean, for example, this obsession with meritocracy in China. You know, I see that, you know, teaching Chinese students. You know, if you ask about where are they from, you know, you see this immense sort of social mobility in China. You can get ahead in China. Anyone can get ahead. And, you know, that's very cultural also. You know, that's been for a thousand, 2,000 years they've had this examination system getting on for. you know, where, you know, people got to the top and they worked for the... You know, the elite were meritocratically chosen. Now, the British elite, they're just a bunch of, like, demobilized warlords, you know.
turns.zh: 而且中国确实有这些优势。比如说，中国对择优精英制（meritocracy）的这种执念。我在教中国学生时就能看到这一点。如果你问他们来自哪里，你会看到中国存在极其巨大的社会流动性。在中国你可以出人头地，任何人都可以出人头地。这也非常有文化根源：他们已经有一两千年的科举考试制度，人们可以凭此一路向上……你知道，进入顶层、为……你知道，精英是通过择优方式选拔出来的。相比之下，英国的精英呢，他们不过是一群解甲归田的军阀罢了。

turns.en: You know, the creative destruction thing reminds me, I wanted to ask you at least one AI question.
turns.zh: 你知道，说到创造性破坏，这提醒了我，我至少想问您一个关于人工智能（AI）的问题。

turns.en: Oh, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，好啊好啊。

turns.en: Probably more than that.
turns.zh: 可能还不止一个。

turns.en: But, so.
turns.zh: 不过，那么……

turns.en: The creative destruction argument is that if you have elites, incumbents in power, they're going to block new things because they want to protect their own sources of wealth. In a place like the U.S., if a local community votes against a new data center, is that democratic empowerment or is that creative destruction? And how do you tell the difference between the two? Yeah, I mean, I think that's... Sorry, not creative destruction, blocking.
turns.zh: 创造性破坏的论点是：如果有一批当权的精英、既得利益者，他们就会阻挠新事物，因为他们想保护自己的财富来源。在美国这样的地方，如果一个当地社区投票反对新建一座数据中心，那这是民主赋权（democratic empowerment），还是创造性破坏？你怎么区分这两者？是的，我是说我觉得那是……抱歉，不是创造性破坏，是“阻挠”。

turns.en: Just destruction. Yeah, I think.
turns.zh: ……是“阻挠破坏”。是的，我觉得……

turns.en: No, I think economic destruction.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得是“经济破坏”。

turns.en: I think that's, you know, that's... People are rightfully anxious about the consequences of AI for their jobs and their.
turns.zh: 我觉得那是……你知道，人们对人工智能给自己工作带来的后果感到焦虑是情有可原的，包括他们的……

turns.en: Incomes and standard of living. You know, for me, the whole.
turns.zh: ……收入和生活水平。你知道，对我而言，这整个……

turns.en: You know, there's an interesting analogy between what's happening, I think, what's going to happen in the Industrial Revolution.
turns.zh: ……我认为当下正在发生的事、以及即将发生的事，与工业革命之间存在一个很有意思的类比。

turns.en: You know, if you look at the Industrial Revolution, the mechanization.
turns.zh: 你知道，如果你看看工业革命，那场机械化……

turns.en: In Britain, for example, the mechanization of, you know, cotton spinning... weaving you know what was the impact of that on weavers wages they tanked by two-thirds you know their wages fell by two-thirds you know what was their reaction the luddites you know they got hammers and they tried to smash up the machinery you know and so isn't that what's happening now and i think The analogy to falling wages.
turns.zh: 比如在英国，棉纺的机械化……织布。你知道那对织工工资的影响是什么吗？他们的工资暴跌了三分之二。那他们的反应是什么？卢德分子（the Luddites）——他们拿起锤子，试图砸烂机器。那么，现在发生的不正是同样的事吗？而且我认为，与工资下跌的类比……

turns.en: Is probably pretty apt also.
turns.zh: ……大概也相当贴切。

turns.en: If you think about that fact that I was talking about earlier about what's happened to people without a college education, the evidence suggests that the biggest factor explaining that is the diffusion of computers, computers displacing relatively unskilled workers. So we're still trying.
turns.zh: 如果你想想我前面谈到的那个事实——没有大学学历的人遭遇了什么——证据表明，解释这一现象的最大因素就是计算机的普及，计算机取代了相对低技能的工人。所以我们仍然在努力……

turns.en: To recover from that, and now we're faced with AI.
turns.zh: ……从那一次冲击中恢复过来，而现在我们又面临人工智能。

turns.en: Well, I'm sure.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想也是。

turns.en: Speaking more of AI, you know, in the last several weeks, there's been, like, this sense of dread and despair that's come over the math community because of these breakthroughs and probably math professors at University of Chicago, some of your colleagues. Like, would you be surprised if we had something that truly resembled a big neo-Luddite movement in America or in the modern world?
turns.zh: 多说说人工智能吧。你知道，过去几周里，数学界因为那些突破而弥漫着一种恐惧和绝望的情绪，芝加哥大学大概也有一些数学教授、你的一些同事。如果美国、或者现代世界真的出现了某种真正意义上的新卢德主义（neo-Luddite）运动，你会感到惊讶吗？

turns.en: Yeah, I'd be surprised. I mean, I, well.
turns.zh: 是啊，我会感到惊讶。我是说，我，嗯……

turns.en: Aren't we still the same people, you know, like, Have we changed?
turns.zh: 我们难道不还是同样的人吗？我们变了吗？

turns.en: Yeah, I don't know. It's a good question. It's hard to know what it's going to accumulate into.
turns.zh: 是啊，我不知道。这是个好问题。很难说这些会累积成什么。

turns.en: I mean, I think there's going to be, science fiction aside, there's going to be big improvements in productivity like there was in the Industrial Revolution.
turns.zh: 我是说，我认为——把科幻放一边——将会出现生产率的巨大提升，就像工业革命时那样。

turns.en: It's how you spread that.
turns.zh: 关键在于你如何把这些……

turns.en: Benefits to society that's going to be sort of critical.
turns.zh: ……收益散布到整个社会，那才是至关重要的。

turns.en: I don't know. That's a good question. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我不知道。这是个好问题。是的。

turns.en: I read an interesting paper of yours in prepping for this, which is talking about the sort of like, maybe it's like the economist obsession with stamping out market failure.
turns.zh: 在为这期节目做准备时，我读了您一篇很有意思的论文，讲的是——也许可以这么说——经济学家对消除市场失灵（market failure）的那种执念。

turns.en: So there are things that economists don't like. They hate rent control. They hate, many of them think.
turns.zh: 有些东西是经济学家不喜欢的。他们讨厌租金管制（rent control）。他们讨厌——很多人认为……

turns.en: That like you got to be really careful about like not setting minimum wages too high. Union power, like maybe some of that like isn't optimal. But as you point out, like these... maybe these are like the least worst outcomes. Can you talk a little bit about maybe some of this sort of monomaniacal obsession with economists of getting rid of these and how they can be costly?
turns.zh: ……你必须非常小心，不能把最低工资定得太高。工会力量，也许其中一些并不是最优的。但正如您指出的，这些也许是最不坏的结果。您能不能谈谈经济学家这种近乎偏执的一门心思——非要除掉这些东西——以及它们为什么可能代价高昂？

turns.en: Yeah, I think the problem there is economists don't understand the politics of these things.
turns.zh: 是啊，我认为问题在于经济学家不理解这些事情背后的政治。

turns.en: Yeah, say more about that.
turns.zh: 是的，再多说一点。

turns.en: You know, I mean, you know, there's an economic argument for having trade unions if you have monopsony power. You know, if employers have market power setting wages, trade unions can actually increase wages But, you know, leaving that aside, I think if you look at, you know, think about Western European societies where trade unions have played important political roles, like in Scandinavia, they've been enormously important in creating and sustaining inclusive jobs.
turns.zh: 我是说，如果存在买方垄断势力（monopsony power），那么设立工会在经济上是有理由的：如果雇主在设定工资上拥有市场势力，工会实际上可以提高工资。但撇开这一点不谈，我认为如果你看看西欧社会——工会在那里扮演过重要的政治角色，比如在斯堪的纳维亚（Scandinavia）——工会在创造和维持包容性的……

turns.en: Political institutions.
turns.zh: ……政治制度方面极为重要。

turns.en: So you can't think about the economics without thinking about the politics.
turns.zh: 所以你不能只谈经济而不谈政治。

turns.en: I guess that's a lot of our research.
turns.zh: 我想这就是我们研究的大量内容。

turns.en: So, like, you get rid of the union, and maybe you get a brief uptick in GDP, but then a couple years later, everyone is alienated, and then it all falls apart.
turns.zh: 所以说，你把工会干掉，也许GDP会短暂地小幅上升，但几年之后所有人都产生了疏离感，然后一切就分崩离析了。

turns.en: That's part of the mess we're in now.
turns.zh: 这就是我们现在所处乱局的一部分原因。

turns.en: It's not just about the diffusion of computers, but also de-unionization, the sort of elimination of unions in this country.
turns.zh: 这不仅仅是计算机普及的问题，还有“去工会化”（de-unionization），也就是这个国家里工会被消灭的过程。

turns.en: That's also.
turns.zh: 那也是……

turns.en: part of what's created this sort of alienation, it seems to me.
turns.zh: ……在我看来，是造成这种疏离感的一部分原因。

turns.en: We're going to have to insert the monopsony box into this episode. It's an ongoing joke we have on the podcast. Whenever anyone says monopsony, we're supposed to have a sound effect. I don't know if we actually do it, because I never listen to the post-edited versions.
turns.zh: 我们得在这期节目里插入“买方垄断”音效盒子了。这是我们播客上一个长期的玩笑：每当有人说 monopsony（买方垄断），我们就应该配一个音效。我不知道我们是不是真的这么做了，因为我从来不听后期剪辑过的版本。

turns.en: We can't listen to our own voices. It's too painful.
turns.zh: 我们没法听自己的声音，太痛苦了。

turns.en: I said that completely independently.
turns.zh: 我说那句话完全是独立想出来的。

turns.en: Just in terms of interesting research, is there anything you're working on now using AI that would have been impossible before you could deploy large language models?
turns.zh: 就有趣的研究而言，您现在有没有在做什么借助人工智能的研究，是在能够部署大语言模型（large language models）之前根本不可能做的？

turns.en: Absolutely. Tell us what.
turns.zh: 当然有。那您就说说看是什么。

turns.en: Give us a preview. So one project we're working on is... So one of the things that we're sort of fascinated with at the moment is just trying to understand the role of kind of ideas in politics.
turns.zh: 给我们先预告一下。我们正在做的一个项目是……我们目前非常着迷的一件事，就是试图理解观念（ideas）在政治中所扮演的角色。

turns.en: You know, like, I mean, you know....
turns.zh: 你知道，就像，我是说，你知道……

turns.en: Economists and even political scientists tend to focus very much on sort of material interests. But I think ideas like your your notion of like how the world should be and what's a legitimate way to organize political authority.
turns.zh: 经济学家、甚至政治学家都往往非常关注物质利益。但我认为，观念——比如你对世界应该是什么样子的看法，以及什么样的方式才是组织政治权威的正当方式——

turns.en: And that's very important. You know, we think so.
turns.zh: ……这一点非常重要。我们是这么认为的。

turns.en: So what we're doing is basically using AI to sort of, you know, We've digitized enormous amounts of works of political philosophy, and we're using that to look at the impact of philosophical ideas on action in 17th century British politics. So you might say, 17th century British politics, why the heck are we doing that? That's the era of Thomas Hobbes and John Locke and some of these immensely important works of political philosophy.
turns.zh: 所以我们在做的基本上就是用人工智能——我们已经把大量政治哲学著作数字化了，我们正在用它来考察17世纪英国政治中哲学观念对行动的影响。你也许会问：17世纪英国政治，我们干嘛要研究那个？那可是托马斯·霍布斯（Thomas Hobbes）和约翰·洛克（John Locke）的时代，产生了一些极其重要的政治哲学著作。

turns.en: So we're trying to understand how did those arguments affect the way people acted and argued and behaved. So that would have been impossible without AI.
turns.zh: 所以我们想弄明白的是，那些论辩如何影响了人们的行为、论争和举动。没有人工智能，这是不可能做到的。

turns.en: I'm really excited about this stuff.
turns.zh: 我对这些东西真的很兴奋。

turns.en: I think the opportunity to sort of use quantitative approaches on huge bodies of text and score them on various dimensions is like a very exciting.
turns.zh: 我认为，能够用定量方法处理海量文本、并在多个维度上给它们打分，这是一个非常令人兴奋的……

turns.en: Aspect of AI. Yes. No, I agree.
turns.zh: ……人工智能的面向。是的。不，我同意。

turns.en: I mean, you know, I tend to think, I'm trying to think of AI as something that compliments me and makes me more productive.
turns.zh: 我是说，我倾向于把人工智能看作某种能够补足我、让我更高产的东西。

turns.en: And, you know, I hope that's generally true.
turns.zh: 而且，我希望这大体上是对的。

turns.en: All right, we have one minute left.
turns.zh: 好了，我们还剩一分钟。

turns.en: Oh, gosh.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。

turns.en: Why do nations fail?
turns.zh: 国家为什么会失败？

turns.en: Because they create extractive institutions. There's still a minute left.
turns.zh: 因为它们建立了攫取性制度。还有一分钟呢。

turns.en: We didn't even need that minute.
turns.zh: 我们连那一分钟都没用上。

turns.en: What should we be watching out for in terms of the U.S.? In terms of?
turns.zh: 在美国这个问题上，我们应该留意些什么？留意什么？

turns.en: The U.S.
turns.zh: 美国。

turns.en: Yeah, what should we be looking out for?
turns.zh: 对，我们应该留意什么？

turns.en: Well, I think we should look at how the election goes next month and how properly things are conducted. And also, I think we should look at whether people try to undermine the kind of you know, the sort of the, you know, undermine, I don't know what.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为我们应该看看下个月的选举如何进行，看看事情是否被妥善地执行。而且我认为，我们还应该看看是否有人试图破坏那种……你知道，试图破坏——我不知道……

turns.en: The right word is, the veracity of the election.
turns.zh: ……该怎么说才对——选举的真实性（veracity）。

turns.en: I think what we've seen in this country in the last few years is enormous attempts to undermine, you know, elections. You know, there's very little evidence, for example, in this country that elections are improperly done.
turns.zh: 我认为过去几年我们在这个国家看到的，是大量试图破坏选举的行为。比如说，在这个国家几乎没有证据表明选举存在舞弊。

turns.en: Or they're fiddled or they're fake or they're whatever.
turns.zh: 或者说选举被操纵了、是假的、或者别的什么。

turns.en: So I think this language attempting to convince people of that is very damaging to the institutions.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，这种试图让人们相信选举有问题的言论，对制度是极具破坏性的。
